newsitem.title: SPAIN: Rumasa chief cleared in decade-old Spanish scandal.
newsitem.headline: Rumasa chief cleared in decade-old Spanish scandal.

text.p: Spain's High Court cleared financier Jose Maria Ruiz-Mateos on Thursday of all fraud charges connected to the collapse of his Rumasa business empire, putting to rest a scandal that rocked Spain 14 years ago.

The court said, in documents made public on Thursday, it had found evidence of account tampering and unpaid taxes, but had not found Ruiz-Mateos guilty, nor any of the four other former Rumasa directors who been charged in the high-profile case.
Ruiz-Mateos, an eccentric and controversial public figure who once fled custody by donning a wig, hailed the verdict as vindication of a 14-year struggle against what he said was unfair persecution.

"It has ended. Private satisfaction. Here I am with my family, with my wife, my children and weeping. I pardon the whole world from my heart despite everything they have made us suffer," he told local radio shortly after hearing the verdict.
The Rumasa case started on February 23, 1983 when the former Socialist government took over the holding company after it crashed spectacularly with losses of 300 billion pesetas ($2 billion).
The state had charged that Rumasa directors had falsified documents to deceive authorities about its financial health.

The High Court agreed that Rumasa figures had been inflated and there was some trickery evident in "the wilful arithmetical errors made in the liquidation sums", but neither finding was criminal nor fraudulent under the new penal code.

At the time of the expropriation, Rumasa was Spain's biggest business group by far, with 20 banks and some 700 companies including hotels, insurance firms, the Dry Sack sherry producer and department store chain Galerias Preciados.

Ruiz-Mateos, 65, came from a humble background in the poorer south with little education, but managed to build up an empire and be accepted by the exclusive Opus Dei religious group, which at the time permeated Spain's elite business community.

He started in business in 1961 with $3,000 and seven workers. By 1982, he had made Rumasa into a group representing almost four percent of Spain's gross domestic product and employing 65,000 people. The state broke up the group and sold the parts after the collapse.
He has aired his claims of injustice in the case with regular publicity stunts, appearing on courthouse steps dressed as Superman, a bullfighter and a pirate.

Ruiz-Mateos had always called his trial a nuisance deflecting attention from the real issue, which he said was the state's unfair expropriation and sell-off of Rumasa at often bargain-basement prices.
His exploits have at times defied belief.
He caused a sensation by putting on a wig in a bathroom during court hearing and fleeing to Germany but was extradited back in 1985 on charges of falsifying documents.
He scuttled his first trial by firing his lawyer just as it was to begin, and further delayed it by getting elected to the European parliament in June 1989.

When his fellow European deputies voted to lift his immunity in February 1991, he appeared to have nowhere left to turn, but he appealed to the European Court of Justice in Strasbourg and it ruled that Spanish justice had not given him a fair trial.
The current trial was delayed four times as Ruiz-Mateos excused himself for health reasons. It finally began on February 10.
